headline: 15 of 29 files should not be opened. 4 more need a closer look.

files.name: image_is_really_a_program.jpg
rationale: Rule 2: 2 high-severity finding(s) with usable confidence (content_is_executable, image_not_an_image).

findings.title: File contains a program, whatever it is named
findings.plain: Regardless of its name, the contents of this file are a Windows program.
findings.why: The operating system decides what to do with a file partly by its contents. A program named .txt is still a program.
findings.action: Do not open or run this file. Send it to IT.

findings.title: File is not the picture it claims to be
findings.plain: This file is named like an image (.jpg) but its contents are not image data — they look like a Windows program.
findings.why: Renaming a program to end in .jpg is the oldest trick there is. Some programs open files by content rather than by name, so the real type is what matters.
findings.action: Do not open it. Send it to IT.
findings.evidence: magic bytes b'MZ\x90\x00echo' detected as pe

files.name: invoice‮gpj.exe
rationale: Rule 2: 2 high-severity finding(s) with usable confidence (name_bidi_override, name_executable_extension).

findings.title: Filename uses a right-to-left override character
findings.plain: This file's name contains an invisible character that makes the name display backwards from a certain point, so what you see is not what the file is called.
findings.why: The only practical use of this character in a filename is to make a program look like a picture or a document.
findings.action: Do not open this file. Send it to IT.

findings.title: File is a program or script
findings.plain: This is a .exe file — the computer treats it as something to run, not something to read.
findings.why: A submission that is a program should be expected (a computing assignment) or refused. It should never be opened by double-clicking to 'see what it is'.
findings.action: If this is a programming assignment, open it in a text editor. Otherwise do not open it at all.

files.name: office_renamed_program.docx
rationale: Rule 2: 1 high-severity finding(s) with usable confidence (content_is_executable).
Note: inspection was also incomplete, so there may be more than is listed.

findings.title: File contains a program, whatever it is named
findings.plain: Regardless of its name, the contents of this file are a Windows program.
findings.why: The operating system decides what to do with a file partly by its contents. A program named .txt is still a program.
findings.action: Do not open or run this file. Send it to IT.

findings.title: Not actually an Office document
findings.plain: This file is named like an Office document (.docx) but its contents are not in any Office format.
findings.why: A file whose real type does not match its name is either broken or deliberately disguised. Either way the Office checks could not run.
findings.action: Do not open it by double-clicking. Ask the student to re-send it.

files.name: pdf_launch_action.pdf
rationale: Rule 2: 1 high-severity finding(s) with usable confidence (pdf_launch_action).

findings.title: PDF runs something automatically when opened
findings.plain: This PDF is set up to do something on its own the moment it is opened, before you click anything.
findings.why: Automatic actions are how a PDF starts working without the reader doing anything. Some are harmless (jump to a page, play a sound); the mechanism is also the standard delivery step for PDF exploits.
findings.action: Open it in a browser's built-in PDF viewer, which sandboxes it, or ask IT.

findings.title: PDF tries to launch another program
findings.plain: This PDF contains an instruction to start another program on your computer.
findings.why: There is no legitimate reason for a coursework PDF to launch an application. This is a direct execution attempt.
findings.action: Do not open this file. Send it to IT.

files.name: pdf_javascript.pdf
rationale: Rule 2: 1 high-severity finding(s) with usable confidence (pdf_javascript).

findings.title: PDF runs something automatically when opened
findings.plain: This PDF is set up to do something on its own the moment it is opened, before you click anything.
findings.why: Automatic actions are how a PDF starts working without the reader doing anything. Some are harmless (jump to a page, play a sound); the mechanism is also the standard delivery step for PDF exploits.
findings.action: Open it in a browser's built-in PDF viewer, which sandboxes it, or ask IT.

findings.title: PDF contains JavaScript
findings.plain: This PDF contains JavaScript — program code that runs inside the PDF reader.
findings.why: Very few documents need JavaScript; interactive forms are the main honest use. In student work it is unusual, and it is the component most PDF exploits rely on.
findings.action: Do not open it in Adobe Reader. A browser PDF viewer is much safer, or ask the student for a plain export.

files.name: Assignment.pdf.exe
rationale: Rule 2: 1 high-severity finding(s) with usable confidence (name_double_extension).

findings.title: File is disguised with a double extension
findings.plain: This file is named to look like a .pdf document but actually ends in .exe, which the computer runs as a program.
findings.why: Windows hides known file extensions by default, so 'essay.pdf.exe' appears in the folder as 'essay.pdf'. Double-clicking runs a program.
findings.action: Do not open this file. Send it to IT.

files.name: archive_double_extension.zip
rationale: Rule 2: 1 high-severity finding(s) with usable confidence (archive_double_extension).

findings.title: Entry is disguised with a double extension
findings.plain: The archive contains a file named like a document but ending in .exe, which the computer will run as a program.
findings.why: Windows hides known extensions by default, so 'essay.pdf.exe' shows up as 'essay.pdf'. Double-clicking it runs a program instead of opening a document.
findings.action: Do not open this archive. Send it to IT.

files.name: archive_path_traversal.zip
rationale: Rule 2: 1 high-severity finding(s) with usable confidence (archive_path_traversal).

findings.title: Archive entry escapes its own folder
findings.plain: One of the files inside this archive is set to unpack somewhere outside the folder you unzip it into.
findings.why: This is how an archive overwrites a file elsewhere on the computer — a startup script or a configuration file — the moment it is extracted. There is no legitimate reason for a student submission to do this.
findings.action: Do not extract this archive. Send it to IT.

files.name: archive_with_program.zip
rationale: Rule 2: 1 high-severity finding(s) with usable confidence (archive_executable_member).

findings.title: Archive contains a runnable file
findings.plain: The archive contains installer.exe, which the computer treats as a program or script rather than a document.
findings.why: Student coursework rarely needs to ship a runnable program. When it does — a computing class, a game project — this is expected; otherwise it is the most common way malware arrives in a submission.
findings.action: If this is not a programming assignment, do not open it. If it is, open it in a text editor rather than running it.

files.name: image_polyglot.png
rationale: Rule 2: 1 high-severity finding(s) with usable confidence (image_polyglot).

findings.title: Another file is hidden inside this image
findings.plain: After the picture data ends, this file contains a ZIP archive.
findings.why: One file that is both a picture and an archive opens as a picture for you and as an archive for whatever the attacker points at it. Nothing legitimate produces this.
findings.action: Do not open this file. Send it to IT.

files.name: office_remote_template.docx
rationale: Rule 2: 1 high-severity finding(s) with usable confidence (office_external_attachedtemplate).

findings.title: Document links out to a remote template
findings.plain: The document is configured to load a template from another location when it opens.
findings.why: Remote template loading is one of the few ways a document that contains no macros of its own can still fetch and run one. It is a well-known phishing technique and almost never appears in student work.
findings.action: Do not open this document normally. Show the link target to IT.

files.name: office_with_macro.docm
rationale: Rule 2: 1 high-severity finding(s) with usable confidence (office_macro_present).

findings.title: Document contains a macro project
findings.plain: This document has macros — small programs stored inside the document that can run when it is opened.
findings.why: Macros are the single most common way a document infects a computer. Some legitimate coursework uses them (spreadsheet classes, accessibility templates), but a macro in an essay is not normal.
findings.action: Do not open this in Word or Excel. If you must read the text, open it in a viewer that does not run macros, or ask IT.

files.name: archive_zip_bomb_shape.zip
rationale: Rule 2: 1 high-severity finding(s) with usable confidence (archive_bomb_ratio).

findings.title: Entry expands to a wildly larger size
findings.plain: One entry is 47.8 KB on disk but claims to unpack to 48.0 MB (1,029 times larger).
findings.why: This is the signature of a decompression bomb: a tiny file that fills the disk or exhausts memory when opened.
findings.action: Do not extract this archive.

files.name: image_large_appended.jpg
rationale: Rule 2: 1 high-severity finding(s) with usable confidence (image_large_appended_data).

findings.title: A large amount of data is stored after the picture
findings.plain: The end of the picture data is more than 256 KB from the end of the file, so this file carries a substantial amount of something else.
findings.why: Image viewers stop at the end of the picture. Hundreds of kilobytes of invisible trailing content is not something a camera or an editor produces.
findings.action: Do not open this file. Send it to IT.
findings.evidence: no jpeg terminator within the last 262144 bytes

files.name: office_dde_field.docx
rationale: Rule 2: 1 high-severity finding(s) with usable confidence (office_dde_field).

findings.title: Document contains a DDE field
findings.plain: This document contains an instruction that asks another program to run when the document opens.
findings.why: DDE fields were widely used to launch commands from Word documents without any macro at all. Modern Office blocks them by default, but not every version does.
findings.action: Do not open this document. Send it to IT.

files.name: links_suspicious.txt
rationale: Rule 3: one medium-severity finding (url_punycode_host).

findings.title: Link uses a lookalike internationalised domain
findings.plain: A link in this file points at a domain written with characters that can imitate ordinary letters.
findings.why: Punycode domains are how 'аpple.com' (with a Cyrillic а) is made to look like 'apple.com'. It is a phishing technique.
findings.action: Do not click the link. Type the address you meant to visit instead.

findings.title: Link points at a bare IP address
findings.plain: A link in this file goes to a numeric address rather than a website name.
findings.why: Legitimate sites almost always use names. A bare IP avoids domain reputation checks and is common in malicious links — though it is also how someone links to a machine on the school network.
findings.action: Check with IT before following it.

findings.title: Link is shortened and hides its destination
findings.plain: This file contains 1 shortened link(s) whose real destination is not visible.
findings.why: A shortened link could go anywhere. Students use them constantly, so this is context rather than an accusation.
findings.action: Preview the link before clicking it.

files.name: archive_password_protected.zip
rationale: Rule 3: one medium-severity finding (archive_encrypted).
Inspection was incomplete; treat the result as a lower bound.

findings.title: Archive is password protected
findings.plain: This archive is locked with a password, so the scanner could not look inside it.
findings.why: Password-protected archives are a standard way to smuggle files past scanners, because nothing — including antivirus — can read the contents. It is also, often, a student who read a tutorial. Either way it has not been checked.
findings.action: Do not open it. Ask the student to re-send the work without a password.

files.name: office_embedded_object.docx
rationale: Rule 3: one medium-severity finding (office_embedded_object).

findings.title: Document has other files embedded inside it
findings.plain: There are 1 file(s) packaged inside this document.
findings.why: Embedding is how a document carries a payload without looking like it does — but it is also how someone attaches a spreadsheet to a report. The embedded files were listed, not opened.
findings.action: Do not double-click the embedded object. Preview the document in a read-only viewer instead.

files.name: pdf_appended_payload.pdf
rationale: Rule 3: one medium-severity finding (pdf_appended_data).

findings.title: Extra data is hidden after the end of the PDF
findings.plain: There are 4,100 bytes of content after the point where this PDF officially ends.
findings.why: A PDF reader stops at the end marker, so anything after it is invisible when you open the file — which is exactly why payloads get stored there.
findings.action: Do not open this file. Send it to IT.

files.name: broken_upload.zip
rationale: Rule 1: the file could not be fully inspected (archive_corrupt). Absence of findings here is not evidence of safety.

findings.title: Archive could not be opened
findings.plain: This ZIP file is damaged or is not really a ZIP file, so its contents could not be listed.
findings.why: A file that will not open cannot be checked. It may simply be a broken upload, but a damaged container is also a way to hide contents from scanners.
findings.action: Ask the student to re-send the file. Do not try to repair it yourself.
findings.evidence: File is not a zip file

files.name: archive_nested_deep.zip
rationale: Rule 4: only 1 weak signal(s) found; not enough to warrant caution.

findings.title: Archive contains other archives
findings.plain: This archive contains 1 further archive(s) inside it.
findings.why: Nesting archives is a routine way to make automated scanners give up before they reach the payload. It is also just how some people package folders.
findings.action: The scanner looked inside up to 3 levels. Anything deeper was not checked.

findings.title: File is empty
findings.plain: This file contains no data at all.
findings.why: An empty submission is a failed upload, not a threat.
findings.action: Ask the student to submit it again.
